newsitem.title: JAPAN: Election looms, Japan's LDP woos new party.
newsitem.headline: Election looms, Japan's LDP woos new party.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party, uncertain of a simple majority in expected general elections, wooed a new reformist party on Sunday to join a post-election coalition.
The offensive to lure a partner came shortly after it became certain that Hashimoto would call general elections next month.

Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama confirmed recent news reports that Hashimoto was expected to dissolve the Lower House on the first day of an extraordinary parliamentary session on Friday and hold general elections on October 20.
"I no longer deny the reports. I feel 99.9 percent certain (the reports are correct)," Kajiyama, the prime minister's right-hand man, told a seminar late on Saturday.
Although Hashimoto agreed last week with leaders of the two junior coalition partners to convene the parliamentary session on September 27, he has been silent on snap polls.

Many analysts and politicans believe the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), the biggest group in the three-party coalition, would not be able to secure a simple majority in the 500-seat Lower House after the snap polls to rule the nation on its own.
"We want to win a simple majority or 251 seats. But that's very difficult," LDP secretary general Koichi Kato told a televised talk show on Sunday.
Political analyst Minoru Morita predicted that none of the parties including two conservative blocks -- the LDP and the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) -- would win a simple majority.
"I think the LDP will win slightly more than 200 seats while the Shinshinto gets slightly less than 200," Morita said.

The LDP was most likely to forge an alliance with the Democratic Party which was expected to be formed soon by rebels from the New Party Sakigake and Social Democratic Party, the two other members of the current coalition, he said.
"We are hoping to work together with the Democratic Party... We must ask for it," LDP's Kato said.
But the leader of the new party was cool to the offer.
"I don't deny the possibility of our party having a swing vote," said Yukio Hatoyama, the founder of the Democratic Party.
"But we may sit in the opposition camp," he added.
Analysts including Morita predicted that the Democratic Party could garner around 50 lower house seats and hold a swing vote in parliament.
If the LDP failed to persuade the Democratic Party, it would have to turn to others such as possible defectors from the Shinshinto, they said.
Last week top government spokesman Kajiyama floated the idea that the Shinshinto join hands with the LDP.
"On the issue of drafting a law to cope with Japan's national security for example, there are more within the Shinshinto that share the same view as compared to the Social Democrats," he said.
"Why not join hands if the Great Ship Japan was in danger of sinking," Kajiyama said, adding that he did not expect a stable government to emerge after elections.
"At any rate, the new coalition government will remain unstable and weak," he said.
